title: Small community forums and hobby sites cannot afford age-verification compliance and are shutting down
affected_user: Volunteer-run and small-business operators of niche forums, hobby communities, and content sites with UK users or users in US states with age-gating laws (roughly half of US states by 2026)
job_to_be_done: Keep a small user-generated-content site online while meeting age-assurance and risk-assessment obligations under the UK Online Safety Act and a patchwork of US state laws
current_process: Operator reads Ofcom guidance / state statutes themselves, attempts a written risk assessment, evaluates commercial age-verification vendors priced for large platforms, or decides to geoblock, close, or scale back the site
what_fails: Rules are vague ('commercially reasonable methods'), differ by state in thresholds and definitions, carry fines up to GBP 18M / 10% of turnover, and require vendor integrations that are not economical for a site with no revenue; operators choose closure over liability
failure_frequency: A platform hosting ~300 small forums shut down with only 2-3 surviving in near-original form (Big Brother Watch report, cited by PrivacySavvy 2026); Green Living Forum and Dads With Kids closed Jan 2025 (EFF, 2025-08). Per-site compliance cost estimates not found.
cost_of_failure: Loss of entire communities and their archives; for operators, fines up to GBP 18M or 10% global turnover under UK OSA (per PrivacySavvy/EFF). Hard per-forum cost figures not found.
existing_workaround: Geoblock UK/affected states, require login and self-declaration, shut down, migrate to Discord/Reddit which handle verification centrally, or wait for OS/device-level age signals (Colorado proposal, some state laws)
who_pays_today: Operators (unpaid volunteer time, hosting), commercial age-verification vendors (Yoti, Persona, etc.) paid by large platforms; small sites mostly pay in closure rather than dollars

sources.note: Summarizes Big Brother Watch report: OSA made small community forums too hard to run; a host of ~300 forums shut down with only 2-3 surviving
Documents small forums (parenting, green living, Linux gaming) shutting down or scaling back rather than face vague, expensive compliance; names Green Living Forum and Dads With Kids closures
Roughly half of US states now require some form of age gating with widely varying scope, thresholds and enforcement, a major obstacle for nationwide operators
Vendor guide noting most state laws mandate verification without specifying qualifying technologies; some cite 'commercially reasonable methods'
House of Lords opened an inquiry into OSA age-check vendors and breaches in late July 2026

firsthand_evidence: The Green Living Forum publicly announced it would close within the week in January 2025 rather than attempt OSA compliance; Dads With Kids closed the same month (paraphrased from EFF coverage). No direct r/sysadmin thread surfaced in results.
key_unknowns: No hard per-site compliance cost figure found; unknown how many US small sites have closed vs. geoblocked; FTC Feb 2026 policy statement on minimal data collection for age checks (reported by a vendor) not verified against FTC release; status of several state laws under NetChoice injunctions is in flux.
technical_unlock: Privacy-preserving age attestation (zero-knowledge / device-level age signals, EU age-verification app, state-level OS signals) is being standardized, which could let a small site accept a cheap signed age claim instead of running its own ID checks; an open-source, self-hostable OSA/state-law risk-assessment and age-gate kit for forum software (Discourse, phpBB, XenForo) is feasible for a solo developer.
why_now: UK OSA age-check duties took effect July 2025; US state laws roughly doubled in count through 2026; Lords inquiry (July 2026) and vendor breaches have raised scrutiny; device-level age signal proposals (Colorado) and app-store age laws began in 2026.
existing_solutions: Yoti, Persona, AgeWallet, IDScan.net, VerifyMy (priced for mid/large platforms); Reddit/Discord handle it centrally; Cloudflare-style geoblocking; no widely adopted small-forum toolkit identified in results.

title: Document-plus-selfie KYC is being defeated at scale by cheap virtual-camera injection and deepfake kits
affected_user: Fraud and compliance teams at fintechs, neobanks, crypto exchanges, online lenders, and marketplaces that onboard customers remotely with document + liveness selfie checks
job_to_be_done: Confirm that a remote applicant is a real, present human who matches a genuine government ID before opening an account or extending credit
current_process: Third-party IDV vendor (Persona, Onfido/Entrust, Sumsub, Jumio, etc.) runs document capture, OCR, and selfie liveness; results reviewed automatically with manual review on flags
what_fails: Attackers bypass the camera entirely with virtual-camera injection and feed deepfaked faces or AI-forged documents; liveness checks designed for presentation attacks do not detect injection; forged digital documents now exceed physical forgeries
failure_frequency: Group-IB documented 8,065 biometric injection attempts against a single financial institution's digital loan onboarding Jan-Aug 2025 (reported Jan 2026); Entrust 2026: deepfakes are 1 in 5 biometric fraud attempts, injection attacks +40% YoY; Sumsub 2025-26 report: deepfake fraud +1,100% 2024-25
cost_of_failure: Fraudulent accounts lead to credit losses, mule accounts, and regulatory exposure; LexisNexis (Mar 2026) puts synthetic-identity-related global losses at $20-40B annually (vendor estimate). Per-institution figures not found.
existing_workaround: Add NFC chip reads of passports/IDs, device attestation, bank-account linking, manual video calls, additional data checks (phone/email risk), or accept higher fraud rates and tighten credit
who_pays_today: Financial institutions pay IDV vendors per verification plus fraud losses; vendors (Entrust/Onfido, Sumsub, iProov, Group-IB, Signicat) sell injection-detection add-ons

sources.note: Aggregates Sumsub 2025-26 (+1,100% deepfake fraud 2024-25), Entrust 2026 (1 in 5 biometric fraud attempts are deepfakes, injection +40%), and Group-IB Jan 2026 (8,065 injection attempts at one FI Jan-Aug 2025)
Vendor explainer of three injection/bypass vectors; cites MIT Technology Review April 2026 finding 22 public Telegram channels selling virtual camera injectors and deepfake kits from ~$30
Vendor claim that a working KYC bypass costs roughly $5; treat as marketing
Academic paper on agentic microservice framework for deepfake and document fraud detection in KYC pipelines; confirms problem framing, no prevalence data
Vendor stat roundup; cites Onfido/Entrust finding digital document forgeries are 57% of document fraud and Signicat deepfake share rising from 0.1% to 6.5% of fraud attempts in 3 years

firsthand_evidence: No firsthand fraud-team complaint surfaced in results; the closest primary observation is Group-IB's documented 8,065 injection attempts against one institution and MIT Technology Review's April 2026 investigation of Telegram kit sellers (both via secondary summaries).
key_unknowns: Headline figures conflict widely (deepfakes 11% of fraud vs 1 in 15 attempts; growth 1,100% vs 2,100%) and nearly all come from vendors; no independent measure of bypass success rate per vendor; unclear how much of the problem hits small fintechs vs large banks.
technical_unlock: Device/platform attestation (Apple App Attest, Android Play Integrity, WebAuthn/passkeys) and NFC chip reading of e-passports/mDLs give cryptographic signals that do not rely on camera pixels; an open-source injection-detection or attestation layer for small IDV integrations is plausible for a solo developer, though competing with funded vendors is hard.
why_now: Deepfake/injection kits became commodity ($5-$30) via Telegram in 2025-26; vendor telemetry shows injection attacks overtaking presentation attacks; mobile driver's licenses and EU digital identity wallets are rolling out as an alternative trust anchor.
existing_solutions: Entrust/Onfido, Sumsub, Persona, Jumio, iProov, Signicat, Group-IB Fraud Protection, DuckDuckGoose, Corsound, Zyphe; NFC-based verification; SentiLink for synthetic identity

title: Data brokers ignore or reject consumer deletion requests and most have not processed California DROP requests
affected_user: Consumers (especially stalking/harassment victims, public-facing workers, Californians using DROP) and privacy-conscious individuals trying to remove personal data from hundreds of brokers
job_to_be_done: Get personal information (address, phone, relatives, people-search profiles) deleted from all data brokers and keep it deleted
current_process: Submit opt-outs broker-by-broker via web forms/email, or pay a removal service (DeleteMe, Optery, Incogni); Californians can file once via CalPrivacy's DROP (live since Jan 1, 2026; brokers obligated from Aug 1, 2026)
what_fails: Brokers deny requests at high rates, demand excess information to verify, and re-populate profiles; in DROP, only about 25% of 654 registered brokers had reported processing requests as of CalPrivacy's August 2026 update; enforcement so far targets registration failures rather than ignored deletions
failure_frequency: Data brokers reported 58.0M deletion requests in a year and refused nearly 900,000; 22 brokers denied more than 90% of deletion requests (Control D analysis of 2024 California filings). ~500,000 Californians signed up for DROP by Aug 2026.
cost_of_failure: Consumers pay $100-$300/yr for removal services; for brokers, $200 per unprocessed DROP request per day; registration fees rising to $9,500 for 2027. Physical-safety harm for stalking victims not quantified in results.
existing_workaround: Paid removal subscriptions, manual recurring opt-outs, DIY spreadsheets of broker URLs, filing CCPA complaints with CalPrivacy, DROP for California residents
who_pays_today: Consumers (DeleteMe/Optery/Incogni subscriptions), employers buying executive-removal services, brokers paying CalPrivacy fees, state budget for DROP platform

sources.note: Analysis of California broker filings: 58.0M deletion requests, ~900,000 refused, 22 brokers denied >90% of requests (2024 metrics)
CalPrivacy: ~500,000 Californians signed up; ~25% of 654 brokers reported processing requests; 99.9% of consumers had profile deleted by at least one broker
Brokers must access DROP every 45 days from Aug 1, 2026 and report status within 45 days; audits start 2028
CalPrivacy penalized LocateSmarter, Cybba and SalesIntel Research for failing to register; enforcement so far centers on registration
Governor's office on first state action against a broker that required personal information before honoring opt-outs
Delete Act regulations approved; 545 brokers registered as of Jan 1, 2026 per related CalPrivacy materials

firsthand_evidence: No Reddit firsthand account surfaced in results (search budget exhausted before a direct r/privacy query returned threads). CalPrivacy's own update implicitly concedes most brokers had not reported processing DROP requests two weeks after obligations began.
key_unknowns: Independent verification of broker deletions (vs self-reported) does not exist until 2028 audits; no published count of DROP complaints or failed deletions; unclear how quickly deleted profiles re-appear; 2024 refusal figures predate DROP.
technical_unlock: DROP creates a single public roster of 654 brokers and a machine-readable request/response channel; a Playwright-driven verification service that re-scans people-search sites for a user's profile after a DROP request and generates CalPrivacy complaints is feasible with the founder's stack. Delete Act regulations also forbid brokers from contacting consumers to verify, simplifying automation.
why_now: DROP went live Jan 1, 2026; broker processing obligations started Aug 1, 2026; $200/request/day penalties now apply; CalPrivacy began penalizing brokers in 2026; other states (Texas, Oregon, Vermont) have broker registries.
existing_solutions: DeleteMe, Optery, Incogni, Kanary, Privacy Bee, Mozilla Monitor; CalPrivacy DROP; Control D broker report

title: Tenant and employment background checks attach the wrong person's records and disputes take longer than the housing or job decision
affected_user: Renters and job applicants (disproportionately people with common names, name changes, or sealed/expunged records); secondarily small landlords and HR teams relying on screening reports
job_to_be_done: Pass a tenant or employment screen that accurately reflects one's own record, and get errors corrected before the opportunity is lost
current_process: Landlord/employer orders a report from a consumer reporting agency (Checkr, HireRight, TransUnion SmartMove, RentGrow, etc.); applicant sees the report only via pre-adverse-action notice; disputes go to the CRA (30-day reinvestigation) and separately to the furnisher/court
what_fails: Name-only or loose matching merges records of different people; civil cases get listed as criminal; outdated evictions beyond seven years persist; corrections take up to 30 days while the apartment or job offer is gone; same error recurs on the next report because the underlying court/agency record is unfixed
failure_frequency: CFPB tenant-screening snapshot: ~26,700 complaints Jan 2019-Sep 2022, nearly two-thirds alleging false/misleading/outdated information leading to rejection; ~4,500 complaints alleged CRAs failed to correct errors within 30 days (CFPB Nov 2022 via Cooley/Consumer Finance Monitor). 2025-26 CFPB updates not found.
cost_of_failure: Lost housing or job offer; FCRA statutory damages up to $1,000 plus actual damages per violation (law-firm guides); application fees and moving costs; 'a correction does not restore the opportunity you lost' (law-firm commentary)
existing_workaround: Pull one's own reports in advance, contact court clerks to fix source records, hire FCRA attorneys on contingency, carry court dispositions to showings/interviews, file CFPB complaints
who_pays_today: Applicants (fees, lost opportunities), FCRA plaintiff law firms (contingency), landlords/employers paying screening vendors $20-$60 per report, CRAs' dispute-handling staff

sources.note: Summarizes CFPB reports: ~26,700 complaints, nearly two-thirds alleging false/misleading/outdated info; ~4,500 alleging failure to correct within 30 days
Law-firm summary of CFPB findings that screening info is often rife with errors, incomplete or outdated
CFPB consumer guidance on disputing with both the screening company and the furnisher and filing CFPB complaints
Press coverage: sloppy background checks preventing renters from securing housing
FCRA law firm describes recurring wrong-person criminal record cases from similar-identity matching, and an airline offer rescinded after a civil case was listed as criminal
Vendor roundup of 2026 complaint statistics for background screening

firsthand_evidence: An FCRA firm recounts a client whose airline job offer was rescinded after a civil case appeared in the criminal section of the report (paraphrased). No 2026 Reddit threads surfaced in results.
key_unknowns: No 2025-2026 CFPB complaint counts found (CFPB capacity has been reduced); unknown share of errors attributable to name-only matching vs stale court data; whether AI-driven tenant screening (e.g., algorithmic scores) is adding new error modes.
technical_unlock: Courts increasingly expose online dockets; a pre-application 'self-screen' that pulls public records for a consumer and generates dispute letters with court-disposition evidence is buildable with Playwright/Python; FCRA gives a private right of action which creates a payer (plaintiff firms).
why_now: CFPB enforcement capacity dropped in 2025-26 while screening vendors added AI matching; fair-chance laws expanded; tenant-screening fee rules in some states; no clear 2026 trigger found.
existing_solutions: Consumer Attorneys, Weiner & Sand and other FCRA firms; CFPB complaint portal; Checkr/HireRight candidate portals; Upturn research; TransUnion SmartMove

title: Patients still wait months to years for their own medical records despite HIPAA right-of-access and information-blocking rules
affected_user: Patients, caregivers, and personal-injury/disability attorneys requesting records; also small practices and release-of-information staff who must respond
job_to_be_done: Obtain a complete copy of one's medical records (or get them sent to another provider) within the legal 30-day window, in electronic form, at a reasonable fee
current_process: Patient submits a written request or portal message; practice routes to medical records staff or an outsourced ROI vendor; records delivered on paper/CD/fax or through a portal, often with per-page fees; complaints go to HHS OCR (HIPAA) or ASTP/ONC (information blocking)
what_fails: Requests sit unanswered or are delayed well beyond 30 days; portals embargo results (radiology report holds flagged by ONC as likely information blocking); front-desk staff do not know the rules; fees and format limits are used to deter requests
failure_frequency: OCR has reached 55 Right of Access settlements since 2019, the latest (Azul Vision, Aug 27 2026) involving a nearly two-year wait; ONC information-blocking portal logged ~1,600 complaints by Feb 2026 and over 2,500 by July 2026, most filed by patients and most naming providers
cost_of_failure: Delayed care transitions and legal claims; OCR penalties $50,000 (Azul Vision 2026) to six figures (OHSU 2025, reported as $70,000 or $200,000 by different sources); OIG penalties up to $1M per information-blocking violation for developers/networks
existing_workaround: Repeated calls, OCR complaints, hiring attorneys or record-retrieval services, asking the new provider to request records provider-to-provider, downloading piecemeal from multiple portals
who_pays_today: Patients (fees, time), law firms paying record-retrieval vendors, providers paying ROI vendors (Ciox/Datavant, MRO, Verisma), HHS enforcement budgets

sources.note: OCR's 55th Right of Access settlement; Azul Vision pays $50,000 after patient waited nearly two years
Details of Azul Vision settlement and two-year corrective action plan
Right of Access initiative continuing in 2026; proposed rule to shorten response deadline from 30 to 15 days
HHS actively enforcing information blocking; ASTP/ONC issued notices of potential non-conformity to EHR developers in Feb 2026
ONC identified blanket portal embargoes on radiology reports as likely information blocking, not covered by Preventing Harm exception
ONC complaint portal over 2,500 submissions by July 2026, most from patients, most naming providers; front-desk and ROI processes a common source
Compliance vendor review of 55 enforcement actions asking whether providers are getting the message

firsthand_evidence: The Azul Vision case (OCR, Aug 2026) documents a patient who waited nearly two years for records; most ONC information-blocking complaints are filed by patients against providers (paraphrased from coverage).
key_unknowns: Complaint counts (1,600 vs 2,500) may use different measures; no data on median patient wait time nationally; whether HTI-5 proposed rule and 15-day deadline will be finalized; share of failures at small practices vs health systems.
technical_unlock: FHIR patient-access APIs are now mandatory for certified EHRs, so a patient-side tool that aggregates records across portals and auto-generates dated OCR/ONC complaints when deadlines lapse is buildable; a provider-side request tracker that enforces 30-day clocks is a simple SaaS for small practices.
why_now: ASTP/ONC began issuing non-conformity notices and HHS announced increased enforcement resources in 2026; HTI-5 proposed Dec 2025; proposed 15-day deadline expected around Nov 2026; 55 OCR settlements establish precedent and penalty expectations.
existing_solutions: Datavant/Ciox, MRO, Verisma (ROI vendors); Fasten Health, Health Gorilla, 1up Health, Particle Health (patient/record APIs); OCR and ONC complaint portals; HIPAA Journal trackers

title: Finance staff at SMBs cannot verify that a payment instruction from a 'known' executive or vendor is genuine as voice and video are cloned
affected_user: Accounts-payable staff, controllers and bookkeepers at small and mid-size businesses, accounting firms, and title/escrow companies; their fraud insurers
job_to_be_done: Confirm, before releasing a wire or changing vendor bank details, that the request truly came from the authorized person
current_process: Email approval chains, phone call-backs to known numbers, occasional dual-approval policies; many SMBs rely on recognizing the executive's voice or seeing them on a video call
what_fails: Voice and video are no longer proof; cloned CFO/CEO voices and deepfake video calls have led to multimillion-dollar wires (Arup ~$25M in 2024; a Swiss businessman transferring several million CHF after voice-cloned calls in 2026); SMBs lack formal out-of-band verification and vendor-change controls
failure_frequency: FBI IC3 2025: 24,768 BEC complaints, adjusted losses just over $3B, second most costly crime type; AI-involved BEC losses exceeded $30M with 22,364 AI-related complaints (~$893M) overall; AI share widely believed undercounted
cost_of_failure: Average BEC loss on the order of $120K per complaint (derived: ~$3B / 24,768); individual deepfake incidents $2.3M-$25M; FBI guidance to call numbers already known, never numbers given in the request
existing_workaround: Call-back policies, code words, dual approval, bank positive-pay, cyber/crime insurance, staff training; many SMBs have none of these formally
who_pays_today: SMBs (losses, insurance premiums), banks (recovery efforts), security-awareness vendors (KnowBe4 etc.), deepfake-detection vendors, cyber insurers

sources.note: Reports IC3 2025 BEC figures (24,768 complaints, just over $3B) and AI-augmented BEC trends
Executive commentary that voice recognition is no longer a valid verification control
Accounting-profession guidance on stopping deepfake payment fraud; recounts Arup case
SEC 2026 warning on AI impersonation fraud
Case narrative of a $2.3M wire moved in one afternoon via CEO deepfake; vendor-adjacent source
Summary of IC3 2025 report: 1,008,597 complaints, $20.877B losses; first year account takeover broken out (4,700 complaints, $359.7M)

firsthand_evidence: Swiss businessman (2026) transferred several million francs after a series of calls with what he believed was a trusted partner, later confirmed a voice clone (paraphrased from vendor/press summaries). FBI guidance explicitly tells businesses to call back on known numbers.
key_unknowns: FBI data does not disaggregate deepfake BEC from classic BEC; the widely repeated '40% of BEC is AI deepfakes' claim is unverified vendor marketing; no SMB-specific loss breakdown found; how many SMBs have any out-of-band verification policy is unknown.
technical_unlock: Cheap cryptographic out-of-band approval (passkey/WebAuthn-signed payment approvals, signed vendor bank-change attestations) can replace voice recognition; a lightweight approval app that integrates with QuickBooks/Bill.com/Ramp is within a solo developer's reach, though incumbents (Bill.com, Ramp, banks) are adding similar controls.
why_now: Real-time voice cloning became consumer-grade in 2025-26; IC3 2025 report (released 2026) first broke out account-takeover and AI-involved losses; SEC issued 2026 AI impersonation warning; insurers tightening social-engineering coverage terms.
existing_solutions: KnowBe4 training, Bill.com/Tipalti vendor-change workflows, bank positive pay, Reality Defender/Pindrop/Netarx deepfake detection, Trustmi, Nudge Security; FBI call-back guidance

title: Synthetic identities pass credit-union and small-lender onboarding and are only discovered as charge-offs
affected_user: Credit unions, community banks, auto-finance companies, and fintech lenders without dedicated fraud analytics teams
job_to_be_done: Distinguish a fabricated identity (real SSN + fake name/DOB, often built over months) from a thin-file but genuine applicant at account opening and credit decision
current_process: Credit bureau pull, KYC/CIP check, OFAC screen, sometimes a fraud score; thin-file applicants approved at small limits and limits raised on good payment history (which synthetic identities exploit before bust-out)
what_fails: Synthetic identities look like legitimate new-to-credit consumers; small lenders lack cross-institution velocity data; losses booked as credit losses rather than fraud, so the problem is under-measured and under-resourced
failure_frequency: TransUnion (Oct 2026): US lenders carried ~$2.4B synthetic identity exposure at end of June 2026, $1.5B of it in auto lending; Celent/Zest AI survey: 93% of lenders say fraud contributes to credit losses, 82% saw fraud losses rise in 2026, 61% name synthetic identity as fastest-growing; SentiLink: 15% of synthetic identities target credit unions and CUs extend more credit to them than to real identities
cost_of_failure: Projected unsecured credit losses from synthetic identity >$3.1B in 2026 (up from $1.8B in 2020, per one study); credit unions report seven-figure losses from identity-related incidents (ProSight, on ATO)
existing_workaround: SSA eCBSV checks, manual review of thin-file applicants, lower starting limits, third-party synthetic scores (SentiLink, Socure), CUSO-shared fraud lists
who_pays_today: Lenders (charge-offs), fraud vendors (SentiLink, Socure, TransUnion TruValidate, LexisNexis), SSA eCBSV fees, NCUA examination costs

sources.note: TransUnion report: ~$2.4B synthetic identity exposure at US lenders as of June 2026, $1.5B in auto lending
Celent study commissioned by Zest AI: 93% of lenders say fraud drives credit losses; 82% report increase in 2026; 61% cite synthetic identity as fastest-growing
Vendor white paper: 15% of synthetic identities target credit unions; CUs issue more credit to synthetics than to real identities
Trade association: credit unions reporting seven-figure losses from account-takeover incidents driven by social engineering
Coverage of study finding synthetic identity fraud surging as criminals use AI to generate identities and documents
Statistics roundup including projection of >$3.1B unsecured losses in 2026 vs $1.8B in 2020

firsthand_evidence: No firsthand credit-union fraud-officer complaint surfaced; nearest is ProSight's association-level report of seven-figure CU losses and the Celent survey of lenders (both secondary).
key_unknowns: Loss estimates range from ~$3B to $30-35B annually depending on vendor and definition; no NCUA-sourced breakdown for small institutions; unclear what share of small lenders already use a synthetic score; ability of a new entrant to access consortium data is doubtful.
technical_unlock: SSA eCBSV API (SSN-name-DOB verification) is available to permitted entities and consortium velocity signals are the key data; without proprietary data a solo founder could only build thin wrappers, so this is a problem to note rather than attack directly unless partnered with a CUSO.
why_now: TransUnion's October 2026 report and the 2026 Celent survey show synthetic fraud rising fastest among fraud types as generative AI lowers cost of fabricated documents; auto lending exposure concentrated.
existing_solutions: SentiLink, Socure, TransUnion TruValidate, Experian, LexisNexis Risk, Zest AI, SSA eCBSV, Alloy, Effectiv

title: Merchants cannot prove an AI shopping agent was authorized by the cardholder, and no chargeback rules cover agent-initiated purchases
affected_user: Online merchants and payment-ops teams accepting checkouts initiated by AI agents (ChatGPT/Codex via Visa, Mastercard Agent Pay), plus bot-management and fraud teams distinguishing legitimate agents from scrapers
job_to_be_done: Accept an agent-initiated order with confidence that the human principal approved it within scope, and win the dispute if the cardholder later denies the purchase
current_process: Merchant accepts tokenized credential (Visa Intelligent Commerce / Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agentic Tokens) and relies on network-provided signatures; otherwise treats agent traffic like any bot and blocks or allows it; disputes handled under existing card-not-present rules
what_fails: Authorization today assumes a human approves each transaction; agent mandates and scope limits exist in protocols (AP2, TAP) but neither Visa nor Mastercard has published a binding chargeback rule for agent disputes; an authorization within a spending limit can still fail at settlement; no jurisdiction has enacted agentic-commerce regulation as of mid-2026
failure_frequency: unknown; agent-initiated checkout only became broadly available June 10, 2026 (Visa + OpenAI; Mastercard Agent Pay for Machines)
cost_of_failure: unknown; merchants bear card-not-present chargebacks and fraud screening costs; potential for agent purchases to be repudiated or for legitimate agents to be blocked as bots
existing_workaround: Block all agent/bot traffic, require human re-confirmation via email/SMS, rely on network tokens and accept dispute risk, limit agent purchases to low-value items
who_pays_today: Merchants (chargebacks, bot-management vendors), card networks and PSPs building agent rails, OpenAI/Google/Perplexity as agent platforms, identity vendors (xident, etc.)

sources.note: Describes Visa Intelligent Commerce scoped tokens and Mastercard Agentic Tokens bound to agent, merchant scope and consent
Notes Visa and Mastercard ship scoped-credential rails but neither has published a binding chargeback rule for agent disputes
June 10, 2026 Visa-OpenAI announcement: tokenized credentials power agent checkout in ChatGPT/Codex with spending limits enforced before authorization

IMF note: traditional authorization (KYC, MFA) assumes human users explicitly approving transactions; frames delegation/authorization layer on AP2, OAuth 2.0, OIDC with scope, revocation, auditability
Agent Identity Protocol proposal for verifiable delegation across MCP and A2A
Runtime authorization for resources acquired by AI agents
Observes that an authorization within a limit can still fail when funds must move; no jurisdiction has enacted agentic-commerce regulation as of mid-2026

firsthand_evidence: None found; evidence is protocol documentation, trade commentary and academic proposals rather than merchant complaints. Problem is structurally real but early.
key_unknowns: Actual volume of agent-initiated purchases and dispute rates; whether networks will issue agent-specific chargeback rules in 2026-27; whether IETF agent-authorization/transaction-token drafts progress; how many merchants have seen a repudiated agent purchase.
technical_unlock: Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay publish verifiable agent signatures; OAuth/OIDC delegation extensions and AP2 mandates give a merchant-side verification surface; an open-source middleware that validates agent signatures and logs mandates for dispute evidence is buildable, but the market is nascent and dominated by networks/PSPs.
why_now: Visa-OpenAI and Mastercard agent rails launched June 2026; AP2 and Trusted Agent Protocol published 2025-26; IMF and academic work on agent delegation appeared 2026.
existing_solutions: Visa Intelligent Commerce / Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay, Google AP2, OpenAI Agentic Commerce Protocol, Stripe agent tooling, Cloudflare bot verification, xident
